subject: Banking
title: Iceland's Banking Collapse
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Iceland's Banking Collapse.

hook.text: Iceland's three largest banks grew to 10 times the nation's GDP.

buildup.text: Icelandic banks offered high-interest online savings accounts across Europe.

discovery.text: Total banking assets reached $182 billion for a country with 330,000 people.

twist.text: Iceland let its banks fail and prosecuted 26 bankers. It recovered faster than countries that bailed out their banks.

climax.text: Iceland proved that banking sectors can outgrow their countries.

punchline.text: Banks 10x the GDP. Iceland let them fail and recovered faster than expected.

quiz.question: How did Iceland respond to its banking collapse?
options: Let banks fail and prosecuted bankers

details.summary: Iceland's three largest banks collapsed simultaneously in 2008, owing $85 billion from a country with a GDP of just $14 billion. The crisis bankrupt the nation, destroyed its currency, and led to unprecedented citizen protests and government reform.
details.whyItMatters: Iceland showed what happens when an entire country's banking system grows too large relative to its economy. The government could not bail out banks that owed six times the national GDP.
takeaways: Iceland's banking debts were six times the country's entire GDP
All three major banks failed within a single week in October 2008
Iceland was the only country to prosecute and jail bank executives after 2008

faq.question: How did Iceland's banks get so large compared to the economy?
faq.answer: After privatization in 2003, the banks aggressively expanded internationally, borrowing in foreign markets to fund rapid growth. By 2008, their combined assets were ten times Iceland's GDP, creating a national vulnerability that was impossible to backstop.

faq.question: How did Iceland recover from the banking collapse?
faq.answer: Iceland let the banks fail, imposed capital controls to prevent money from leaving, and prioritized protecting domestic depositors. The country jailed dozens of bankers, reformed its financial system, and experienced one of the fastest economic recoveries in Europe.
